nameStory: The Northern Spreadwing gets its name from its unique resting posture — unlike most damselflies that fold their wings back along their body, spreadwings hold their wings out at about a 45-degree angle, as if they're spreading them to catch the sun. The "Northern" part distinguishes this species from its southern cousins, as it's one of the more cold-tolerant members of its family.
description: The Northern Spreadwing is a slender damselfly with a delicate, graceful appearance typical of its family. These insects are smaller and more fragile-looking than dragonflies, with thin bodies that shimmer with metallic green or bronze tones. Adults typically measure about 1.5 to 2 inches long with narrow, clear wings that they hold at distinctive angles when perched. You'll often see them perched vertically on plant stems near ponds and wetlands, looking almost like tiny jeweled ornaments.

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: When resting, wings are held out at roughly 45-degree angles from the body rather than folded back parallel to the body like most other damselflies

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Slender body with metallic green or bronze sheen that catches the light beautifully, often with darker stripes along the sides

idTips.label: Perching Behavior
idTips.description: Often perches vertically on thin plant stems, gripping with legs that feel surprisingly strong for such a delicate-looking insect

idTips.label: Wing Appearance
idTips.description: Clear, narrow wings that appear almost crystalline in sunlight, with fine dark veining visible up close

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Weak, fluttery flight that's more hesitant and less direct than dragonflies, often staying close to vegetation

habitat: Northern Spreadwings prefer still or slow-moving freshwater habitats like ponds, marshes, and quiet backwaters of streams throughout New England. They're particularly fond of areas with emergent vegetation like cattails, sedges, and water lilies where they can easily perch and hunt for small insects. You'll often find them in slightly acidic waters surrounded by sphagnum moss and other bog plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but numbers are still low. Look for recently emerged individuals with slightly duller colors near breeding waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most visible, actively mating and laying eggs. This is the best time to observe their characteristic spreadwing posture and metallic body colors.
seasonality.fall: Adult numbers decline through early fall as the breeding season ends. Late-season individuals may appear more worn with faded colors.
seasonality.winter: No adults visible; the species overwinters as eggs laid in plant stems near water, waiting for spring warmth to trigger development.

funFact: The genus name 'Lestes' comes from the ancient Greek word for 'thief' — but these delicate damselflies earned this fierce name because they're actually accomplished aerial pirates, snatching tiny flying insects right out of the air with surprising precision despite their seemingly fragile appearance.
confusionNotes: Northern Spreadwings are most easily confused with other spreadwing species in the Lestes genus, but the distinctive 45-degree wing angle separates all spreadwings from other damselfly families. Memory trick: 'Spread wings = spreadwing' — if the wings are angled out instead of folded back, you've found a member of the spreadwing family.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Northern,' this species isn't restricted to the far north — it's found throughout New England and beyond. The common names of spreadwings can be confusing because their ranges often overlap significantly, so habitat preferences and subtle physical differences become more important than geographic names for identification.
compareHints: Among New England's spreadwings, the Northern Spreadwing is distinguished by its preference for more permanent water bodies compared to species like the Swamp Spreadwing which favors temporary pools. It's also generally more metallic in appearance than the Slender Spreadwing and lacks the distinctive amber wing tints of the Amber-winged Spreadwing. The Emerald Spreadwing is similar but typically shows more vibrant green coloration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's spreadwings, the Slender Spreadwing is distinguished by its exceptionally thin body profile and pale blue face coloration.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Spotted Spreadwing is one of the easier ones to identify thanks to its distinctive wing spots.
Among New England's nine Lestes species, Swamp Spreadwings are distinguished by their strong preference for heavily vegetated wetlands and their larger, more robust build.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Amber-winged is distinguished by its wing coloration when present, though this can be subtle.
Among New England's spreadwings, the elegant spreadwing is distinguished by its bronze-brown coloration and medium size.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Emerald Spreadwing stands out for its brilliant metallic green coloration - most others like the Swamp Spreadwing appear more bronze or brown.
Among New England spreadwings, sweetflag spreadwings are distinguished by their preference for heavily vegetated wetlands rather than open water.
